recoveryRoadmap.description: Step-by-step family recovery plan for the first 30 to 365 days after a death or severe incapacity. Use the steps in order and focus on documents, bank access, and claims before broader legal work.

intro.condolence: We are sorry for your loss. This roadmap is designed to reduce confusion and show what matters first.
intro.howToUse: Start with immediate documents and financial access. Then file insurance and benefits claims, complete legal administration, and rebuild the family plan.

startHere: Get certified copies of the death certificate and list every account, policy, and asset.
Pause or cancel auto-payments, subscriptions, and recurring card charges.
Review beneficiaries on life insurance, retirement accounts, and bank accounts.
Notify the employer, bank, insurer, and executor or next of kin about the death.
Collect original wills, deeds, IDs, and policy papers in one secure place.
Check whether there is a trust, power of attorney, or healthcare directive.
Keep a simple log of every call, claim, and appointment.
legalFramework: State probate and estate administration laws
Uniform Probate Code principles in many states
ERISA and employer benefit plan rules
Life insurance and disability contract terms

Federal and state tax return requirements for a decedent's estate

phases.title: Immediate stabilization
phases.focus: Secure documents, money, and legal records before the estate becomes complicated.

keyActions.action: Obtain certified death certificates and keep at least 10 to 15 copies. Count them for bank, insurer, mortgage, hospital, and federal uses.
keyActions.why: Every claim, transfer, and legal filing usually needs a certified copy. Missing copies create avoidable delays.

keyActions.action: Review all joint accounts, beneficiary designations, and transfer-on-death accounts. Confirm which assets pass outside probate and which require formal estate action.
keyActions.why: Some assets move outside probate because of beneficiaries or joint ownership. That is important for the first wave of access and protection.

keyActions.action: Stop recurring charges: mortgage, auto-pay, credit cards, subscriptions, utility bills, and any small automatic payments. Ask the bank for a temporary review if needed.
keyActions.why: Recurring charges can create late fees, damaged credit, and confusion during a family emergency.
keyActions.legalRef: Consumer account terms and bank procedures

keyActions.action: Arrange a safe place for original documents: passport, ID, deed, will, trust records, insurance policies, tax filings, and healthcare directives.
keyActions.why: Originals often move faster than copies when a bank, insurer, or court needs proof.
keyActions.legalRef: Document retention and estate administration practices

keyActions.action: Notify the employer or retirement plan administrator about the death and ask about life insurance, disability, final paycheck, pension, or survivor benefits.
keyActions.why: Employer benefits are often time-sensitive and may be separate from personal insurance policies.

keyActions.action: Contact each insurer and ask for claim forms for life insurance, health insurance, mortgage protection, or disability benefits. Ask whether the claim is subject to a no-fault or contestability review.
keyActions.why: Insurers often need the policy number, beneficiary designation, and death certificate before they can pay benefits.
keyActions.legalRef: Insurance contract terms and state claims rules

keyActions.action: Check whether a will, trust, or power of attorney exists. If there is a court-appointed executor or personal representative, ask for a copy and document all actions.
keyActions.why: A clear chain of authority reduces delays and prevents disputes about who can act on the estate.

criticalMistakes: Not ordering enough certified death certificates. Banks, insurers, and courts often need multiple copies.
Assuming every account goes through probate. Beneficiary designations and joint accounts can bypass probate.
Paying off debts without checking whether a policy or benefit may cover them.
Using the deceased's online banking, cards, or passwords after death without authority.
Ignoring a will, trust, or healthcare directive because the family thinks it is not urgent.
Delaying employer, retirement, and insurer notification because the family does not know the plan details.

legalDeadlines.deadline: As soon as possible; state rules vary
legalDeadlines.consequence: Delay can slow down funeral arrangements, account access, and claim filings.

legalDeadlines.deadline: Usually within a few weeks to a few months after filing all documents
legalDeadlines.consequence: Benefit delays can make daily expenses and debt payments harder to manage.

legalDeadlines.deadline: Use the plan's deadlines and filing instructions immediately
legalDeadlines.consequence: Benefits can be missed if the family waits too long to file.

phases.title: Claims and account transfer
phases.focus: File benefits, move accounts, and identify what is probate vs non-probate property.

keyActions.action: File life insurance claims, retirement benefit claims, and any employer death benefits. Include the death certificate, policy numbers, and beneficiary paperwork.
keyActions.why: Many benefits are time-sensitive and separate from the estate process.

keyActions.action: Move or close the deceased's bank, brokerage, retirement, and savings accounts according to the account terms and beneficiary instructions.
keyActions.why: Accounts without a beneficiary or with a stale title often require formal administration before they can be transferred.
keyActions.legalRef: Bank, brokerage, and retirement account rules

keyActions.action: Review real estate, vehicles, and titled property. Confirm whether a deed or title transfer requires probate, a transfer affidavit, or a title office filing.
keyActions.why: Property transfer questions usually cost time and money if handled late.
keyActions.legalRef: State property and title transfer rules

keyActions.action: Ask the bank or financial institution whether there is a small estate process, summary administration, or transfer-of-asset form available for the estate.
keyActions.why: Some estates are eligible for faster procedures when the assets and debts are modest.

keyActions.action: Document all debts, credit cards, and loans. Ask each creditor whether they have a death benefit, insurance, or debt cancellation process.
keyActions.why: This prevents paying debts twice or missing benefits that belong to the estate or family.

keyActions.action: Start the estate administration process if there is no beneficiary or if the assets require probate. Ask whether a will requires formal appointment of an executor or personal representative.
keyActions.why: A formal court process can be important for property, creditor clearance, and family disputes.

mustHaveDocuments: Life insurance and retirement benefit claim forms
Death certificate and beneficiary documents
Bank and brokerage account details
Real estate deeds and vehicle title papers
Loan and credit card statements
Will, trust documents, and probate papers
List of all assets and liabilities
Tax records and information for the decedent

keyContacts.name: County or state probate court
keyContacts.use: Estate opening, will filing, and executor appointment

keyContacts.name: DMV or title office
keyContacts.use: Vehicle title transfer and property-related paperwork

criticalMistakes: Failing to file benefits before the family sees a bigger cash crunch.
Assuming all money can be accessed without checking beneficiary designations or joint ownership.
Leaving property title questions unresolved while the family is still grieving.
Paying estate debts or creditor claims before checking insurance or asset coverage.
Ignoring beneficiary updates on retirement and insurance accounts.
Waiting to open probate when a clear title or creditor process is required.

legalDeadlines.deadline: File as early as possible and follow plan-specific deadlines
legalDeadlines.consequence: The claim may stall or be denied if the family waits too long or misses required documents.

legalDeadlines.deadline: No universal deadline, but file promptly when probate or court action is required
legalDeadlines.consequence: Delays can increase conflict, cost, and legal risk.

legalDeadlines.deadline: Follow the decedent's final return and estate filing deadlines
legalDeadlines.consequence: Late or missed filings can create penalties and interest.

phases.title: Legal and financial settlement
phases.focus: Finalize estate administration, property transfer, taxes, and debt handling.

keyActions.action: If probate is required, file the necessary court documents and keep a ledger of assets, debts, account activity, and distributions.
keyActions.why: A clear ledger prevents confusion about what belongs to the estate and what has already been distributed.

keyActions.action: File the final tax return for the deceased and any required estate tax or income reporting. Confirm whether the family must file as executor or personal representative.
keyActions.why: The estate may still owe taxes, and the fiduciary has reporting duties. Missing these filings can create penalties and liability.

keyActions.action: Review all loans, credit cards, mortgages, and debts and verify whether there is life insurance or benefit coverage. Do not pay debts blindly.
keyActions.why: Some debt is covered by a policy or a benefit. Other debt remains the estate's responsibility unless it was jointly owned or a co-signer is liable.

keyActions.action: Complete real estate transfer, utility changes, and vehicle title records. Confirm the deed, property tax status, and any mortgage or lien information before sale or transfer.
keyActions.why: Title defects and unpaid liens can block a sale or create disputes later.
keyActions.legalRef: Property title, mortgage, and local government records

keyActions.action: Review healthcare directives, powers of attorney, and any trust terms. Ask whether the family needs to change fiduciary roles or update account mandates.
keyActions.why: The family may need to replace authority on accounts, medical decisions, or financial operations after the loss.

keyActions.action: Protect digital access: email, banking portals, cloud storage, social media, and subscriptions. Save and secure account records in a way that the family can use later.
keyActions.why: Digital accounts often contain critical information and may require a legal process or collaboration with the provider to access safely.
keyActions.legalRef: Digital account terms and privacy law

mustHaveDocuments: Court filings and probate documents
Inventory of estate assets and debts
Final tax returns and estate-related filings
Mortgage, deed, property tax, and title records
Beneficiary and fiduciary records
Healthcare directives and trust documents
Digital account access list and recovery information

keyContacts.name: CPA or tax preparer
keyContacts.use: Final tax return and estate reporting

keyContacts.name: Mortgage or lender
keyContacts.use: Loan status, insurance, and payoff questions

keyContacts.name: Local recorder or property office
keyContacts.use: Deed, title, and property transfer records

criticalMistakes: Confusing probate with non-probate assets. The process is different for titled property and beneficiaries.
Failing to file the final tax return for the deceased or to keep the estate records current.
Selling or transferring property before the title and lien checks are complete.
Ignoring a trustee or fiduciary instruction in a trust or will because the family thinks it is optional.
Leaving digital accounts unmanaged after a death, which can lead to loss of records and access.
Paying debt without checking whether it was covered by a policy, benefit, or insurance asset.

legalDeadlines.deadline: As soon as practical when the estate requires court action
legalDeadlines.consequence: Delays can increase court costs, conflict, and administrative time.

legalDeadlines.deadline: Follow applicable federal and state deadlines for the decedent and estate
legalDeadlines.consequence: Missed deadlines can create penalties and interest.

legalDeadlines.deadline: Address early when a property transfer or sale is being planned
legalDeadlines.consequence: Unresolved liens or unpaid debts can block a clean transfer.

phases.title: Rebuild and protect the family
phases.focus: Protect the surviving family from future disruption by updating plans, beneficiaries, and emergency records.

keyActions.action: Update beneficiary designations on all bank accounts, retirement accounts, life insurance, and investment accounts. Keep a written record of who is named and why.
keyActions.why: Beneficiary designations are often the fastest way to avoid a repeat of this process for the next generation.

keyActions.action: Review the family's existing will, trust, and healthcare plan. Update powers of attorney, executor designations, and emergency care instructions for all adult family members.
keyActions.why: A valid plan reduces uncertainty when a family is under stress. Good planning is not just for older adults; it is for any family with dependents.
keyActions.legalRef: Will, trust, and healthcare planning law

keyActions.action: Build a liquid emergency fund equal to 6 to 12 months of essential household expenses. Keep it in a high-yield savings account or cash reserve rather than locked investments.
keyActions.why: A family cannot manage a sudden crisis without accessible cash.

keyActions.action: Review life, disability, and health insurance needs. Confirm that the surviving family members still have adequate cover for income replacement and healthcare.
keyActions.why: Coverage gaps can create real financial strain later, especially when a household becomes dependent on a single income.
keyActions.legalRef: Insurance policy terms and renewal rules

keyActions.action: Create a single family asset register with account numbers, account types, passwords, document locations, and key contacts. Store one copy securely and share one copy with a trusted fiduciary or family member.
keyActions.why: This turns a stressful crisis into a manageable checklist for the next generation.
keyActions.legalRef: General recordkeeping and estate planning best practices

keyActions.action: Review all legal and financial roles: executor, trustee, agent under power of attorney, and healthcare proxy. Make sure there is a trusted person ready to step in if needed.
keyActions.why: The family should not learn mid-crisis that a role was never appointed or was outdated.

mustHaveDocuments: Updated will and trust documents
Updated beneficiary records on all accounts and policies
Emergency fund plan and cash reserves
Health and life insurance policy review
Power of attorney and healthcare directives
Updated family asset register
Executor or fiduciary information

keyContacts.name: Financial advisor or CFP
keyContacts.use: Cash planning, insurance review, and beneficiary updates

keyContacts.name: Estate planning attorney
keyContacts.use: Wills, trusts, powers, and family planning

keyContacts.name: Insurance broker or agent

criticalMistakes: Not updating beneficiaries after a major life event.
Leaving key roles undefined when a family is already vulnerable.
Failing to review life, health, and disability coverage after a major loss.
Keeping all family records in one place with no trusted backup person.
Not creating a cash reserve before a future emergency hits.
Assuming legal documents do not need a fresh review after a family change.

legalDeadlines.deadline: At least once a year and after changes in family status
legalDeadlines.consequence: Outdated beneficiaries can cause major family and legal confusion.
Gaps in cover can become expensive and disruptive.

legalDeadlines.deadline: After major family changes, marriage, divorce, or children
legalDeadlines.consequence: The family may inherit a plan that no longer reflects their wishes.

glossary.definition: The person named to carry out the terms of a will and handle estate administration.
The legal fiduciary appointed to administer the estate under state law.
The person or entity named to receive an asset or benefit on death.
The court-supervised process for authenticating a will and administering the estate.
A legal arrangement that holds assets for beneficiaries under the terms of a trust agreement.
A document giving another person authority to act on your behalf for legal or financial matters.
A document outlining medical preferences and who can make healthcare decisions.
Ownership that may pass directly to the surviving co-owner without going through probate, depending on the jurisdiction.
An account or asset that can pass directly to a beneficiary outside probate.
A legal claim against property to secure a debt or obligation.
